strengths: WMDD addresses a practically important problem: distilling large image datasets without expensive bilevel optimization. Combining representative feature targets with per-class BatchNorm regularization is a sensible approach.

The reported results are strong across three datasets and multiple compression budgets. At 50 images per class, WMDD achieves 57.6% on ImageNet-1K versus 53.5% for CDA, and 59.4% on Tiny-ImageNet versus 48.7% for CDA (Table 1).

Cross-architecture experiments include both ResNets and vision transformers. The factorial ablation also supports complementary benefits: adding Wasserstein feature matching to PCBN improves accuracy by 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 percentage points across the three datasets (Table 4).

The manuscript provides useful diagrams, qualitative comparisons, repeated-run results, implementation settings, and a code link. It attributes the datasets and principal borrowed methods and acknowledges that distillation can preserve source-data biases.
weaknesses: A substantial baseline discrepancy weakens attribution of the headline gains. At ImageNet-1K 10 IPC, Table 1 reports SRe2L at 21.3%, whereas Table 4 reports the corresponding CE-plus-standard-BN configuration at 35.9%. Against that internal baseline, WMDD improves to 38.1%, a much smaller gain. The manuscript should reconcile these protocols and compare methods under matched teacher, recovery, relabeling, and evaluation settings.

The central mathematical formulation has an unaddressed connection to ordinary clustering. With one source distribution, squared Euclidean transport cost, and freely optimized support weights, Eq. (5) reduces to minimizing average squared distance to the nearest support point: the k-means objective. This does not preclude a useful distillation contribution, but the missing discussion and comparison against k-means centroids inverted with the same PCBN pipeline leave the novelty and necessity of the proposed transport machinery unclear.

The evidence does not isolate an advantage of the Wasserstein metric over MMD. Figure 4 still compares different feature priors—random encoders versus a pretrained encoder—after removing augmentation and FKD. At one support point, squared Wasserstein distance and linear-kernel MMD in the same fixed feature space both target the class mean. Appendix B provides standard discrepancy bounds, without ordering their tightness, and analyzes W1 rather than the implemented squared W2 objective.

The optimization description needs substantive clarification. Algorithm 2 updates the weights but then reuses a transport plan computed with the previous weights for the position update. Its column marginals therefore need not match the new weights. Moreover, simplex projection permits zero weights, while Eq. (11) divides by those weights. The barycenter learning rate, support initialization, and handling of zero weights are unspecified, limiting reproducibility and support for the convergence claim.

The efficiency evidence only partially supports the large-scale claims. Table 3 uses ImageNette at 1 IPC, where the squared-Wasserstein representative is simply the class mean; Table 5 adds Tiny-ImageNet measurements but no ImageNet-1K breakdown. Accounting separately for teacher training, feature extraction, transport computation, recovery, and FKD would make the claimed computational savings assessable.
